one_line: Bridgewater's Applied AI team describes the Vault, a governed corpus of 100M+ unstructured documents, and the lessons from making it useful to both human investors and agents: separate design for each reader, benchmark-driven search, and feeding agent-human synthesis back into the corpus.
summary: Sam Green and Aaron Linsky of Bridgewater explain the Vault, the internal platform that cleans, governs and indexes more than 100 million external and internal documents for investors and agents. They argue that unstructured data needs the same curation and ontology alignment as structured data, and that humans and agents need different things from the same platform: humans want precision and signal, agents want recall, filtering and scale. They report a hand-labelled benchmark of about 200 queries that measured precision at 10 at roughly 60% before agentic search and roughly 90-95% after. They describe a switch to a vector database with cluster-aware filtering to get both speed and recall on date, source and asset filters. They also say adoption came from first migrating users' existing email-style habits (saved searches, collections) before adding new features. The talk closes with an always-on "investor workbench" that proposes topics with evidence, and with the claim that synthesis generated by humans and agents is written back into the corpus so the system compounds. Most numbers are self-reported internal figures without a public eval.

key_ideas.idea: Humans and agents are different consumers of a data platform and need to be designed for separately, though the best outcome is one tool serving both.
key_ideas.detail: Humans have limited reading throughput and need precision and high signal-to-noise; agents are far less precision-sensitive, scale quickly and read much faster. The speakers frame the five retrieval dimensions as recall, precision, filtering, entitlements and scale, and say some matter to people, some to agents, and many to both.

key_ideas.idea: Unstructured data needs the same curation and governance as structured data before agents can use it well.
key_ideas.detail: Bridgewater says no vendor gave enough control, so they built the Vault: over 100M documents from 135 external sources plus internal memos and meeting transcripts, added continuously, and enriched with countries, concepts, markets and especially the time period a document discusses.

key_ideas.idea: Time scoping is the failure mode that matters most for investment questions: a stale source can silently answer a current question.
key_ideas.detail: In the demo, a generic enterprise agent found 15 web sources but used only one or two, and drew on a note about three months old. With the Vault connected, the agent searched an early-October window, found 52 candidates, and used seven in its answer.

key_ideas.idea: Search quality was measured against hand-labelled examples before any tuning, and that baseline made the improvements measurable.
key_ideas.detail: They collected about 200 real questions and hand-picked the best documents, including plausible decoys, in under a week. Precision at 10 started at about 60%, which matched users' complaint that search was bad. After adding agentic search, they report about 90-95%.

key_ideas.idea: Metadata filtering was the first major performance issue; they chose a vector store with cluster-aware filtering over post-filtering or pre-filtering.
key_ideas.detail: Post-filtering is fast but loses recall when relevant documents fall outside the filter; pre-filtering keeps recall but is slow. Turbopuffer's native filtering scores only the nearest clusters that contain matching items, which the speakers say gives near pre-filter recall at post-filter speed.

key_ideas.idea: Scale requirements differ by orders of magnitude between people and agents.
key_ideas.detail: About 300 human users generate roughly 100 queries an hour, while agents can push 100+ queries per second and agent swarms can reach thousands. The same vector store handled both.

key_ideas.idea: Adoption required migrating existing habits first: subscribed email lists became saved searches and folders became saved collections.
key_ideas.detail: Only after researchers had their familiar workflows back did the team add new habits such as cross-corpus questions and topic feeds, then expose the same retrieval through chat, a phone app, Slack, the IDE and a CLI, since agents prefer CLIs. The speakers say this is when they reached product-market fit.

key_ideas.idea: The next step is a proactive, always-on agent that proposes topics to investors with evidence, and their decisions and synthesis are written back into the corpus.
key_ideas.detail: The investor workbench shows a topic card with an agentic summary, the exact evidence the agent used, and a link to deeper research output. When an investor digs in alongside the agent, the resulting synthesis is captured back in the Vault for later retrieval, which the speakers describe as compounding.

techniques.name: Hand-labelled retrieval benchmark before tuning
techniques.how: Collect real user questions (about 200 in their case, built in under a week). For each, hand-pick the best documents, and also include plausible-looking documents that are not right. Track precision at 10 (share of top 10 results that are correct) on every change, so each improvement is measured against the same set.
techniques.when: Before any retrieval tuning, especially when users say search is bad and there is no measurement.

techniques.name: Cluster-aware native filtering in the vector store
techniques.how: Use a vector DB whose filter applies to the nearest clusters that contain matching items, not a post-filter on top-k or a full pre-filter scan. Their target was post-filter latency with pre-filter recall. Filters on date, source and asset are common in production traces, so this is the filter path to optimise first.
techniques.when: When queries routinely carry metadata conditions (as-of date, source, company or asset) and both recall and latency matter.

techniques.name: Infer a time window from the question and scope retrieval to it
techniques.how: Connect the agent to the retrieval layer so it reads the question's time period and searches that window. In the demo the connected agent moved from a three-month-old note to a one-week window containing 52 candidates. The talk describes this at the product level and does not show the exact prompt or filter.
techniques.when: For questions about current or dated events, where a source from months earlier is worse than no source.

techniques.name: Separate human and agent retrieval design
techniques.how: Humans get precision, a high signal-to-noise ratio and feeds or saved searches. Agents get high recall, bulk and high-throughput access. Build both paths on one index instead of one interface for both.
techniques.when: When the same corpus serves analysts and automated agents at very different query rates and reading speeds.

techniques.name: Migrate existing user habits into the new tool first
techniques.how: Map each old habit to a feature before adding new ones: subscribed lists become saved searches, folders become saved collections. Then add cross-corpus questions and topic feeds, and expose the same collections to agents for follow-up actions.
techniques.when: When adoption is low even though the tool is better, because users stick to email and folders.

techniques.name: Write synthesis back into the corpus
techniques.how: When a user and an agent work through a question together, store the resulting analysis as a document in the same corpus, so later retrievals can draw on it. The speakers present this as the mechanism behind compounding.
techniques.when: When each research session produces conclusions that future questions should reuse.

tools: Forecaster (internal, custom model plus foundation models)

numbers.claim: Over 100 million documents in the Vault, with thousands added daily from 135 external sources, plus internal data.
A generic enterprise agent found 15 candidate web sources and used one or two; with the Vault it found 52 candidates in a one-week window and used seven.
Hand-labelled benchmark of about 200 examples, built in under a week.
Precision at 10 was about 60% before tuning and reportedly reached about 90-95% after agentic search (the speaker's wording mixes recall and precision at 10).
Human reading speed is about 300 words per minute, and agents are about 100x faster (about 30,000 words per minute).
Human load is about 300 users and about 100 queries an hour; agents reach 100+ queries per second and swarms can reach thousands.
The Pocket Analyst does hours of research in a few minutes for a few dollars.

hot_takes: Benchmark-first search tuning is the practical lesson here: a small hand-labelled set measured with precision at 10 turned a vague complaint into a number.
Filter strategy is an underrated retrieval bottleneck. Post-filtering loses recall and pre-filtering is slow, so cluster-aware native filtering is the middle ground they chose.
Agents need time-scoped retrieval, not just more or better documents. A stale source is a silent failure for current questions.
Migrating users' existing habits (saved searches, folders) mattered more to adoption than the retrieval quality improvements.
Corporate talk with no sponsor segment, but the metrics are internal and unreproduced, and the 90-95% figure is ambiguous in the transcript. Treat it as directional.

relevance.why: MemoryMesh does hybrid retrieval (BM25 + pgvector) with knowledge buckets. The talk gives a concrete method for measuring and improving that retrieval (labelled benchmark, precision at 10, filter strategy, time-scoped retrieval) that MemoryMesh can reuse.
relevance.action: Build a hand-labelled set of about 200 real queries with decoy documents for MemoryMesh, report precision at 10 for BM25, pgvector and hybrid retrieval, and only then tune filters and weights.

relevance.why: The investor workbench shows a proactive pattern: a card with a summary, the exact evidence behind it and a drill-down, with the outcome captured for later use. This maps onto phone-driven approvals and checkpointed runs in ProsHarness.
relevance.action: Use the summary, evidence and drill-down card layout as a reference for ProsHarness phone approvals, and store each approval decision as a retrievable record.
